content: Otitis externa refers to the inflammation of the external auditory canal. This condition is most commonly caused by bacterial infections, particularly from Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus. Less frequently, fungal infections such as otomycosis caused by Candida albicans and Aspergillus niger can also lead to otitis externa. Additionally, inflammatory dermatoses like eczema, seborrhea, and psoriasis may spread to the ear canal and contribute to the condition. The external auditory canal becomes vulnerable to infection when there are sudden changes in the epithelial environment. These changes may include abrupt shifts in humidity, which can degrade the epithelial barrier, reduce cerumen production, and increase the pH of the canal. Such alterations create a favorable environment for bacterial or fungal pathogens to proliferate. Physical or chemical trauma, such as the use of cotton swabs or other cleaning products, can also predispose the ear canal to infection. Gross pathological findings in otitis externa include erythema of the ear canal, scaling, and shedding of the skin resembling eczema. Swelling of the ear canal is often visible, and in severe cases, cellulitis of the pinna and otorrhea may occur. Otitis externa is classified into acute, chronic, or malignant forms based on the duration, severity, and extent of the infection. It is essential to differentiate otitis externa from other conditions that cause similar symptoms, such as otalgia, ear itching, otorrhea, erythema, edema of the ear canal, hearing loss, ear pressure, and dermatitis. Differential diagnoses include otitis media, infectious myringitis, sinusitis, and Meniere's disease. The annual prevalence of acute otitis externa varies geographically, with approximately 24 cases per 100,000 individuals in the United Kingdom and 140 cases per 100,000 in the Netherlands. Malignant necrotizing otitis externa has an annual case fatality rate of 10–20%. Acute otitis externa is most common in adults aged 65–74 years, while malignant otitis externa primarily affects individuals aged 50 and older, often due to immunocompromising conditions such as diabetes mellitus. Risk factors for acute and chronic otitis externa include activities or conditions that predispose the ear canal to inflammation, such as swimming or excessive moisture exposure. Being female and aged 65–74 years is also a risk factor. Malignant necrotizing otitis externa is associated with immunocompromised states, including chemotherapy and diabetes mellitus. Symptoms of otitis externa typically include pain, itching, and swelling of the ear canal. Chronic or recurrent cases may present with a lack of earwax and accumulation of dead skin, leading to narrowing of the ear canal. Malignant necrotizing otitis externa may manifest with severe ear pain, facial paralysis, difficulty opening the mouth, and trouble swallowing. Laboratory findings consistent with otitis externa include evidence of bacterial or fungal infection. Inflammatory markers such as elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), and white blood cell count may also be present. CT imaging is crucial for diagnosing malignant necrotizing otitis externa, as it reveals the extent of infection beyond the ear canal, including involvement of temporal and intracranial bones. Imaging findings may also demonstrate bone and soft tissue damage, as well as cranial nerve involvement causing facial palsy. Scintigraphic imaging with Technetium-99m or Gallium Citrate Ga-67 can further delineate the spread of infection, with Gallium scans being preferred due to their specificity. Treatment of acute otitis externa involves cleaning the external auditory canal and addressing the infection. Topical therapy is the first-line treatment for uncomplicated cases, while systemic antimicrobials are reserved for infections extending beyond the external canal or in patients with specific host factors. Analgesics such as acetaminophen or NSAIDs, alone or in combination with opioids, are used to manage pain. Prevention of otitis externa focuses on avoiding epithelial damage to the ear canal, which predisposes to infection or dermatitis. This includes minimizing exposure to contaminated water and excessively humid conditions. Preventing recurrence involves identifying the underlying cause, whether infectious or dermatologic, and ensuring appropriate topical or systemic therapy is administered. The prognosis of otitis externa depends on the presence of complications. Acute otitis externa generally has a good prognosis and is often self-limiting, resolving within four days without treatment. Chronic cases lasting more than three months may persist indefinitely without intervention. Malignant necrotizing otitis externa, if untreated, has a poor prognosis due to intracranial complications. However, with treatment, acute and chronic otitis externa have favorable outcomes, while the prognosis of malignant necrotizing otitis externa depends on the severity of complications. Historically, otitis externa was first identified in 1873 by Adam Politzer. Treatment advancements include the development of Burrow's solution in the mid-19th century, the introduction of penicillin in 1940, and the use of corticosteroids like dexamethasone in 1957. The modern use of topical antibiotics, such as ciprofloxacin ear drops, began in 1987.
